objective.text: Make fractions that have the same value. Use a number line, an area model, and multiplying.

big_idea.text: Cut each piece into smaller equal pieces. You get more pieces, but the amount stays the same.

vocabulary.kid_definition: Different fractions that name the same amount.
The top number. It tells how many parts we pick.
The bottom number. It tells how many equal parts make the whole.
One equal part of the whole.
vocabulary.example: In fourths, each unit is 1 fourth.

vocabulary.kid_definition: To cut something into equal parts.
vocabulary.example: Partition the square into 4 equal parts.

intro.hook: Think of a sandwich cut in half. Now cut each half in half again. It is still one sandwich.
intro.why_it_matters: Later we add and subtract fractions. For that, we need pieces of the same size. Today you learn to change the size of the pieces.
intro.link_to_before: You already know halves, thirds, and fourths. You also know how to multiply.
intro.today_goal: Today you will make new fractions that equal 1 half, 1 third, and more.

teaching_flow.title: Cut a sandwich
teacher_says: Think about a sandwich. You cut it in half.
Now you cut each half in half again.
You have 4 pieces. But it is still the same sandwich.
Today we use this idea to make fractions that have the same value.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Warm-up story only. Keep it to 4 short lines, then move on.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up: missing factors
teacher_says: First, a quick warm-up. Each question has a missing factor.
A missing factor is the number that fits in the blank. You find it by thinking: what times this gives that?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source is a timed Sprint. Here it is a short untimed warm-up. Stop after 3 right answers in a row if the child is fast.

source_ref.section: Fluency Practice: Write the Missing Factor

teaching_flow.title: Sharing rice
teacher_says: Now a sharing story. 15 kilograms of rice go equally into 4 containers.
How much is in 1 container? Sharing equally is dividing. 15 divided by 4 is a fraction, and also a decimal.
Then we say 75 hundredths in its simplest form. Use a bigger unit. Think of quarters.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source order: the rice story comes first, then the simplest-form question.

teaching_flow.title: What a fraction really says
teacher_says: A fraction has two parts. The bottom number says how many equal parts make the whole.
The top number says how many of those parts we pick.
Look at this strip. It is 1 whole.
Fold it down the middle. Now there are 2 equal parts.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Replaces the paper folding. Make sure the child says 'equal parts' and 'half'.

teaching_flow.title: Same strip on a number line
teacher_says: Now put the strip on a number line. Zero is on the left. 1 is on the right.
The half mark sits in the middle of zero and 1.
Remember this spot. We will check it again soon.

teaching_flow.title: Cut each half in two
teacher_says: Here is a square. We shade 1 half on the left.
Now cut each half across the middle. Each half becomes 2 smaller parts.
The whole now has 4 equal parts. The shaded part has 2 of them.
So 1 half and 2 fourths cover the same space.
if_child_is_stuck: Count the parts in the whole. Then count the shaded parts.

teaching_flow.title: Same point, same value
teacher_says: Go back to the number line. Mark 2 fourths.
It lands on the same spot as 1 half.
They look different, but they are the same number.

teaching_flow.title: Use multiplying
teacher_says: We can show what happened with numbers.
Each of the 2 halves was cut into 2 parts. So the whole has 2 times 2 parts, which is 4.
The shaded part was 1 half. Now it is 1 times 2 shaded parts, which is 2.
We multiplied the top and the bottom by the same number: 2.
Try again. This time cut each half into 3 parts.
if_child_is_stuck: Multiply the top by 3. Multiply the bottom by 3.

teaching_flow.title: Do it with thirds
teacher_says: Now start with 1 third. The whole has 3 equal parts. 1 part is shaded.
Cut each third into 2 parts. Then try cutting each third into 3 parts.

teaching_flow.title: A fraction with a bigger top number
teacher_says: Now start with 2 thirds. Two of the three parts are shaded.
Cut each third into 2 parts. Each shaded part becomes 2 smaller shaded parts.
Count the shaded small parts. Then count all the small parts.

teaching_flow.title: A fraction bigger than 1
teacher_says: This works for fractions bigger than 1 too.
6 fifths is more than 1 whole. We can draw it with rectangles.
Cut each fifth into 2 parts. Same steps, same rule.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Rectangles are used on purpose, so the child does not think only squares work.

teaching_flow.title: Find the pattern
teacher_says: Look at these fractions: 1 third, 2 sixths, 3 ninths, 4 twelfths.
The top goes up by 1. The bottom goes up by 3.
All of them are the same point on the number line.
The pieces get smaller, but the amount stays the same.

teaching_flow.title: One number, many names
teacher_says: A fraction is one number. It is one point on the number line.
There are infinitely many fractions that name that same point.

explanations.title: Same point on the number line
explanations.text: Fold a strip into equal parts. Use it like a ruler on a number line. Mark 0 and 1. Mark 1 half. Now mark 2 fourths. It is the same point. Fractions that mark the same point are equal.

explanations.title: Cut the shaded part into smaller parts
explanations.text: Shade 1 half of a square. Cut each half across the middle. Now there are 4 equal parts. 2 are shaded. The shaded space did not change. 1 half equals 2 fourths.

explanations.title: Multiply the top and bottom by the same number
explanations.text: When you cut each part into 2 smaller parts, you get 2 times as many shaded parts. You also get 2 times as many parts in the whole. So multiply the top by 2 and the bottom by 2. The value stays the same.

explanations.title: Look for the pattern
explanations.text: Write fractions that equal 1 third: 1 third, 2 sixths, 3 ninths, 4 twelfths. The top goes up by 1. The bottom goes up by 3. The bottom is always 3 times the top.

misconceptions.description: Child thinks the area model works only for squares. The source notes that rectangles are used on purpose to break this rigid idea.

misconceptions.response_text: Squares and rectangles both work. Any whole can be cut into equal parts.

intro.why_it_matters: Fractions work the same way. When the unit is the same, adding is easy. We just count units.
intro.link_to_before: Last time you made equal fractions with smaller units.
intro.today_goal: Today you will add equal fractions on a number line and write the answer in different ways.

teaching_flow.title: Apples plus apples
teacher_says: 1 apple plus 1 apple is 2 apples. The unit is apples.
Fractions work the same way. The unit stays the same. We count how many units.
Today we add pieces of the same size and see the total on a number line.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Warm-up. Keep short. The key idea: the unit does not change when adding like units.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up: halves and fourths
teacher_says: First, remember equal fractions. 1 half equals 2 fourths.
Two fourths are 2 parts of a different unit, but the same amount.

teaching_flow.title: Join 1 third and 1 third
teacher_says: Draw a number line from 0 to 1. Cut it into 3 equal parts. Each part is 1 third.
Start at 0. Jump 1 third. Jump 1 third again.
You land on 2 thirds. Same unit, so the answer is 2 thirds.

teaching_flow.title: Write it as multiplying
teacher_says: 2 jumps of 1 third is 2 times 1 third.
So 1 third plus 1 third equals 2 times 1 third, which equals 2 thirds.
Show 3 fourths the same way. Jump 1 fourth, 3 times.

teaching_flow.title: Three parts: 3 eighths, 3 eighths, 1 eighth
teacher_says: Cut the number line from 0 to 1 into 8 equal parts.
Jump 3 eighths. Jump 3 eighths again. Then jump 1 eighth.
We land on 7 eighths. 3 eighths added 2 times, plus 1 eighth.

teaching_flow.title: Fractions that make wholes: 6 halves
teacher_says: Now go past 1. Mark 0 halves to 6 halves. Cut into 6 equal parts.
2 halves make 1 whole. 4 halves make 2 wholes. 6 halves make 3 wholes.
So 6 halves is 3 times 2 halves, which is 3 wholes.

teaching_flow.title: Between two whole numbers: 8 fifths
teacher_says: Now 8 fifths. 5 fifths make 1 whole. So 8 fifths is 5 fifths plus 3 fifths.
That is 1 plus 3 fifths. We say 1 and 3 fifths.
It is more than 1 but less than 2.

teaching_flow.title: Do it again: 7 thirds
teacher_says: 3 thirds make 1 whole. So 7 thirds has two wholes: 6 thirds.
One more third is left. So 7 thirds is 2 and 1 third.
It sits between 2 and 3.

teaching_flow.title: Story problems
teacher_says: Marisela cut 4 equal ribbons. Each is 5 eighths of a yard. Draw jumps of 5 eighths.
Natalie sawed 5 boards. Each is 9 tenths of a meter. Do the same thing.

teaching_flow.title: Many ways to write the same number
teacher_says: 3 sevenths can be 1 seventh plus 1 seventh plus 1 seventh. It can also be 2 sevenths plus 1 seventh.
Different looking answers can both be right.
Our place value system works the same way. 9 tenths plus 3 tenths is 12 tenths, or 1 and 2 tenths.

teaching_flow.title: Why the number line?
teacher_says: The number line shows the jumps. It shows where the answer sits between whole numbers.

explanations.title: Join lengths on a number line
explanations.text: Mark 0 and 1. Cut the line into equal parts. Each part is a unit fraction. Jump one part, then jump again. Count the jumps. The unit does not change. You are counting units.

explanations.title: Same jump again and again is multiplying
explanations.text: 1 third plus 1 third is 2 times 1 third. 3 eighths plus 3 eighths plus 1 eighth is 2 times 3 eighths, plus 1 eighth. Repeated adding of the same fraction can be written as multiplying.

explanations.title: Wholes hiding inside a fraction
explanations.text: 8 fifths is 5 fifths plus 3 fifths. 5 fifths make 1 whole. So 8 fifths is 1 plus 3 fifths. We say 1 and 3 fifths. It is between 1 and 2.

explanations.title: Place value works the same way
explanations.text: 9 tenths plus 3 tenths is 12 tenths. 10 tenths make 1 one. So 12 tenths is 1 and 2 tenths. 9 elevenths plus 3 elevenths is 12 elevenths. 11 elevenths make 1 whole. So it is 1 and 1 eleventh.

examples.title: 1 third plus 1 third
examples.text: Jump 1 third, then 1 third more. You land on 2 thirds. 1 third plus 1 third equals 2 times 1 third equals 2 thirds.

examples.title: 3 eighths, 3 eighths, 1 eighth
examples.text: Jump 3 eighths, 3 eighths, then 1 eighth. You land on 7 eighths.

examples.title: 6 halves makes 3 wholes
examples.text: Every 2 halves make 1 whole. 3 groups of 2 halves make 3 wholes. 6 halves equals 3.

examples.title: 8 fifths is between 1 and 2
examples.text: 8 fifths is 5 fifths plus 3 fifths. That is 1 plus 3 fifths, or 1 and 3 fifths.

examples.title: 7 thirds is between 2 and 3
examples.text: 7 thirds is 6 thirds plus 1 third. 6 thirds is 2 wholes. So 7 thirds is 2 and 1 third.

examples.title: 4 ribbons of 5 eighths
examples.text: Each ribbon is 5 eighths of a yard. 4 ribbons is 4 times 5 eighths, which is 20 eighths. 8 eighths make 1 yard, so 20 eighths is 2 yards and 4 eighths.

objective.text: Add fractions with different units. Make like units first by making equal fractions.

big_idea.text: You can only add pieces of the same size. Make like units, then add.

vocabulary.kid_definition: Fractions with the same bottom number.
vocabulary.example: 2 eighths and 4 eighths have like units.

vocabulary.kid_definition: Fractions with different bottom numbers.
vocabulary.example: 1 half and 1 fourth have unlike units.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A bottom number that both fractions can change to.
vocabulary.example: 8 is a common denominator for halves and fourths.

vocabulary.kid_definition: Change to bigger units so the fraction uses smaller numbers.

intro.hook: 1 adult plus 3 adults is easy. 1 child plus 3 adults is not. The units are different.
intro.why_it_matters: Fractions with different bottom numbers are like children and adults. We must rename them first.
intro.link_to_before: Last time you added fractions with the same unit. You also made equal fractions.
intro.today_goal: Today you will add fractions with different units. You will use equal fractions to do it.

teaching_flow.title: Can we add a child and an adult?
teacher_says: 1 adult plus 3 adults is 4 adults. Easy.
1 fifth plus 3 fifths is 4 fifths. Same unit, so we can add.
Now 1 child plus 3 adults. Hmm. They are different units.

teaching_flow.title: The big idea: rename to like units
teacher_says: We cannot add children and adults as they are.
But both are people. So 1 person plus 3 people is 4 people.
Fractions work the same way. Rename unlike units as like units. Then add.
Can you add 1 half plus 1 fourth as they are?

teaching_flow.title: 1 half plus 1 fourth, step by step
teacher_says: Draw 1 whole as a rectangle. Cut it into 2 equal parts. Shade 1 half.
Draw a second rectangle the same size. Cut it into 4 equal parts. Shade 1 fourth.
Now cut both rectangles so every part has the same size. Each part is 1 eighth.
1 half is 4 eighths. 1 fourth is 2 eighths.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The area model replaces folding paper. Make sure both rectangles are the same size.

teaching_flow.title: Add the like units, then simplify
teacher_says: Now the units are the same. 4 eighths plus 2 eighths is 6 eighths.
We can make bigger units. 6 and 8 can both be divided by 2. That gives 3 fourths.
So 1 half plus 1 fourth is 4 eighths plus 2 eighths. That is 6 eighths, or 3 fourths.

teaching_flow.title: What happens to the units?
teacher_says: When we made like units, the units got smaller.
There are more units, but the space is the same.
1 half turned into 4 eighths. Each part got cut into smaller parts.

teaching_flow.title: Two unit fractions: 1 third plus 1 half
teacher_says: Cut each half into 3 smaller parts. Cut each third into 2 smaller parts.
The like unit is sixths. 1 third is 2 sixths. 1 half is 3 sixths.
2 sixths plus 3 sixths is 5 sixths.

teaching_flow.title: A bigger top number: 2 thirds plus 1 fourth
teacher_says: Shade 2 thirds in one rectangle. Shade 1 fourth in another.
Make all the units the same size. Each unit is 1 twelfth.
2 thirds is 8 twelfths. 1 fourth is 3 twelfths. Add them: 11 twelfths.

teaching_flow.title: Compare sizes: 2 thirds and 2 fifths
teacher_says: 2 thirds and 2 fifths both have 2 parts. But thirds are bigger than fifths.
The whole is cut into only 3 parts, so each part is bigger.
In fifteenths, 2 thirds is 10 and 2 fifths is 6. So 2 thirds is bigger.
Now add them in fifteenths.

teaching_flow.title: A harder one: 2 sevenths plus 2 thirds
teacher_says: The like unit is twenty-firsts. 2 sevenths is 6 twenty-firsts.
2 thirds is 14 twenty-firsts. Add: 20 twenty-firsts.

teaching_flow.title: Story problem
teacher_says: In Mr. Beck's class, 1 ninth like red. Twice as many like blue. Three times as many like pink.
The rest like green. We find green or pink.

teaching_flow.title: Spot the pattern
teacher_says: 1 third plus 1 seventh is 10 twenty-firsts.
2 thirds plus 2 sevenths has top numbers twice as big. So the answer is twice as big.

teaching_flow.title: Name the lesson
teacher_says: Today we added fractions with unlike units.
We made like units with a rectangle model.

explanations.title: Rename the units, then add
explanations.text: You can add 1 adult plus 3 adults. You cannot add 1 child plus 3 adults. But both are people. So 1 person plus 3 people is 4 people. For fractions, rename unlike units as like units. Then add.

explanations.title: Area model: make the parts the same size
explanations.text: Draw 2 same-size rectangles. Shade 1 half in one. Shade 1 fourth in the other. Cut both so all parts are equal. Each part is 1 eighth. 1 half is 4 eighths. 1 fourth is 2 eighths. Add the shaded parts.

explanations.title: The units get smaller
explanations.text: To make like units, cut parts into smaller parts. There are more units. But the units are smaller. The amount stays the same. Then simplify by grouping into bigger units if you can.

explanations.title: Same top number: compare the units
explanations.text: 2 thirds and 2 fifths both have 2 parts. Thirds are bigger than fifths. A whole cut into 3 parts has bigger parts than a whole cut into 5. In fifteenths, 2 thirds is 10 and 2 fifths is 6. So 2 thirds is more.

objective.text: Add fractions when the sum is between 1 and 2. Write the sum as a whole number and a fraction.

big_idea.text: Make like units, add, then take out the whole if the sum is more than 1.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A fraction whose top number is bigger than its bottom number.
vocabulary.example: 10 eighths is a fraction bigger than 1.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A number made of wholes and a part.
A bottom number that works for both fractions.
vocabulary.example: Eighths is a like unit for halves and fourths.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A smart guess that is close to the real answer.
vocabulary.example: 1 half plus 3 fourths is more than 1.

intro.hook: Is 1 half plus 3 fourths more than 1 whole, or less? Make a guess.
intro.why_it_matters: Many fraction sums are bigger than 1. You need to write them in a clear way.

intro.today_goal: Today you add fractions with sums between 1 and 2.

teaching_flow.title: Guess before you add
teacher_says: Good mathematicians guess first. Is the answer more than 1 or less than 1?
Today we add fractions where the answer lands between 1 and 2.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Short hook. Reinforce estimating before calculating.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up: make one whole
teacher_says: First, a warm-up. I say a fraction. You say the fraction that makes 1 whole.
1 third plus 2 thirds makes 1 whole.

source_ref.section: Fluency Practice: Adding Fractions to Make One Whole

teaching_flow.title: Story: Leslie's milk
teacher_says: Leslie has 1 liter of milk. She drank 2 fifths at breakfast and 1 half at dinner.
Fifths and halves are unlike units. We need like units.
Halves and fifths both fit into tenths.

teaching_flow.title: Estimate: 1 half plus 3 fourths
teacher_says: Look at 1 half plus 3 fourths.
3 fourths is more than 1 half. 1 half plus 1 half is 1 whole.
So the sum will be more than 1.

teaching_flow.title: Make like units
teacher_says: Draw 1 half in one rectangle. Draw 3 fourths in another. Same size.
Cut both so every part has the same size. We need 8 parts in each whole.
1 half is 4 eighths. 3 fourths is 6 eighths.

teaching_flow.title: Add, then pull out the whole
teacher_says: 4 eighths plus 6 eighths is 10 eighths.
That has a top number bigger than the bottom. It is more than 1 whole.
8 eighths make 1 whole. 10 eighths is 8 eighths plus 2 eighths.
So the sum is 1 and 2 eighths. We can also say 1 and 1 fourth, because 2 eighths is 1 fourth.
if_child_is_stuck: How many eighths make 1 whole? Take that many out of 10.

teaching_flow.title: Another sum bigger than 1: 13 tenths
teacher_says: Sometimes the sum is 13 tenths.
10 tenths make 1 whole. 3 tenths are left.

teaching_flow.title: 2 thirds plus 3 fifths
teacher_says: Both addends have a top number bigger than 1. Be careful which parts you bracket.
Like unit: fifteenths. 2 thirds is 10 fifteenths. 3 fifths is 9 fifteenths.
Sum: 19 fifteenths. That is 15 fifteenths plus 4 fifteenths.

teaching_flow.title: 3 eighths plus 2 thirds
teacher_says: Each eighth is cut into 3 parts. Each third is cut into 8 parts. What unit are the small parts?
9 twenty-fourths plus 16 twenty-fourths is 25 twenty-fourths. That is 24 twenty-fourths plus 1 twenty-fourth.
24 twenty-fourths is 1 whole. So the sum is 1 and 1 twenty-fourth.

teaching_flow.title: Notice the patterns
teacher_says: When both fractions are more than 1 half, the sum is more than 1.
Then you change the answer to a whole number and a fraction.
Today's model does not show the total. It only shows the number of units to add.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: We made like units. We added. Then we took out the whole.

explanations.title: Estimate before you add
explanations.text: Compare each fraction to 1 half. 1 half plus 1 half makes 1 whole. If both fractions are more than 1 half, the sum is more than 1. If both are less than 1 half, the sum is less than 1.

explanations.title: Area model: like units, then add
explanations.text: Draw 1 half and 3 fourths in two same-size rectangles. Cut both into eighths. 1 half is 4 eighths. 3 fourths is 6 eighths. 4 plus 6 is 10 eighths. The model shows the units. It does not show the sum.

explanations.title: Take out the whole
explanations.text: 10 eighths has a top number bigger than the bottom number. 8 eighths make 1 whole. 10 eighths is 8 eighths plus 2 eighths. That is 1 and 2 eighths. 2 eighths is the same as 1 fourth, so it is also 1 and 1 fourth.

explanations.title: Use 1 whole to find what is left
explanations.text: Leslie has 1 liter. She drank 9 tenths. 1 whole is 10 tenths. 9 tenths plus 1 tenth is 10 tenths. So she has 1 tenth left. As a decimal, that is 0.1.

objective.text: Subtract fractions with different units. Make like units first with equal fractions.

big_idea.text: Subtracting is like adding. Make like units first, then subtract.

vocabulary.kid_definition: Fractions with the same bottom number.
The answer when you subtract.
A fraction with 1 on top.
A fraction with a top number bigger than 1.

intro.hook: 3 boys minus 1 girl. Can you do it? They are different. But 3 students minus 1 student is easy.
intro.why_it_matters: Fractions with different bottom numbers are like boys and girls. We rename them first.
intro.link_to_before: Last time you added fractions with unlike units. You made like units.
intro.today_goal: Today you will subtract fractions with unlike units in the same way.

teaching_flow.title: Boys, girls, students
teacher_says: 3 boys minus 1 girl. Can you do that? Not really. They are different.
But boys and girls are both students. 3 students minus 1 student is 2 students.
Fractions work the same way. Today we subtract fractions with different units.

teaching_flow.title: Same idea as adding
teacher_says: Last time we added unlike units. We made like units first.
To subtract, we do the very same thing. Make like units. Then subtract.
Can you subtract 1 third from 1 half as they are?

teaching_flow.title: 1 half minus 1 third
teacher_says: Draw 1 rectangle. Cut it into 2 equal parts. Shade 1 half.
Draw another the same size. Cut it into 3 equal parts. Shade 1 third.
Now cut both into parts of the same size. We get 6 units.
1 half is 3 sixths. 1 third is 2 sixths.

teaching_flow.title: Cross out and count

objective.text: Solve two-step word problems with fractions. Draw a tape diagram to help.

big_idea.text: Draw the whole and the parts. Find the missing part by subtracting from the whole.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A long bar split into parts to show a story.
vocabulary.example: A bar for the whole garden.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The whole is the total. A part is one piece of it.
vocabulary.example: The whole garden is 1. George's weeding is a part.

vocabulary.kid_definition: Read the story, draw a picture, then write an equation and a sentence.

intro.hook: A story problem is a puzzle. One piece is missing. Let us find it.
intro.why_it_matters: Fractions show up in real stories. A good picture shows what to do.
intro.link_to_before: You can already add and subtract fractions with unlike units.
intro.today_goal: Today you will solve stories with two steps. You will draw tape diagrams.

teaching_flow.title: Story problems are puzzles
teacher_says: A story problem is a puzzle. It has parts and a whole.
One piece is missing. Our job is to find it.
Today we use pictures to solve stories with two steps.

teaching_flow.title: Read, draw, write
teacher_says: We use three questions. What do I see? What can I draw? What can I conclude?
Then we write an equation and a sentence to answer.

teaching_flow.title: Part or whole?
teacher_says: George weeded some of a garden. Summer weeded some too. Some was left.
The whole garden is 1. Summer's amount is a part.

teaching_flow.title: Two ways to solve
teacher_says: Way 1: start with the whole. Subtract George's part. Then subtract the part that is left.
Way 2: add George's part and the left part first. Then subtract once from the whole.
Both ways are correct. They show the same parts and the same whole.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Numbers of the real problem were lost. The tutor uses 1 fourth, 1 third and 5 twelfths as stand-ins.

teaching_flow.title: Three parts: Jing's money
teacher_says: Jing spent money on pens, markers and pencils. We want the part that is left.
Draw one whole tape. Mark the 3 spent parts. The rest is the question mark.
Add the 3 parts or subtract them one by one. Use like units.

teaching_flow.title: The whole is 2
teacher_says: Shelby has a tube with 2 ounces. The whole is 2, not 1.
She used some for water, some for sky, some for a flag. Some was left.
Find the flag part.

teaching_flow.title: Who sold more?
teacher_says: Jim sold some lemonade. Dwight sold some. Together we know the total.
First find Dwight's amount. Then compare. To find how much more, subtract.

teaching_flow.title: Two times as much
teacher_says: Leonard spent 2 times as much on a gift as on comic books.
On the tape, comic books are 1 unit. The gift is 2 units. Together that is 3 units.
Find how much money is in those 3 units. Then share it into 3 equal parts.

teaching_flow.title: Which picture is better?
teacher_says: You can draw containers. Or you can draw a tape diagram.
With large numbers, there are too many containers to draw. The tape is faster.
A tape diagram shows a part, a part, and a whole. An unknown part has a question mark.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Read. Draw a tape. Find the part and the whole. Then add or subtract.

explanations.title: Part, part, whole with a tape diagram
explanations.text: Draw one long tape for the whole. Split it into parts. Label each part you know. Put a question mark on the part you do not know. Now you can see if you should add or subtract.

explanations.title: Two ways: subtract each part, or add the parts first
explanations.text: Way 1: take each part away from the whole, one at a time. Way 2: add the parts you know into one bigger part. Subtract that from the whole once. Both ways give the same answer.

explanations.title: Two times as much on a tape
explanations.text: If one amount is 2 times as much as another, draw the small amount as 1 unit. Draw the big amount as 2 units of the same size. Together they are 3 units.

objective.text: Add fractions to whole numbers and subtract them from whole numbers. Use equal fractions and the number line.

big_idea.text: Adding keeps the fraction the same. Subtracting makes the whole number part one smaller.

intro.hook: A number line is like a road. Whole numbers are big markers. Fractions are small steps between them.
intro.why_it_matters: Later you will add and subtract mixed numbers. The number line helps you see what is happening.
intro.link_to_before: You know how to add and subtract fractions with unlike units.
intro.today_goal: Today you will add fractions to whole numbers and subtract them from whole numbers.

teaching_flow.title: A trip on the number line
teacher_says: Think of a number line as a road. Whole numbers are big mile markers.
Fractions are small steps between the markers. Today we walk the road.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up
teacher_says: Mixed numbers are a whole number plus a fraction. 3 and 1 half is 3 plus 1 half.
Subtracting is the same road backwards.

teaching_flow.title: Review: unlike units
teacher_says: Jane spent 1 fourth on milk and 3 fifths on a magazine. She spent the rest on candy.
Fourths and fifths are unlike. Make twentieths. 5 twentieths plus 12 twentieths is 17 twentieths.
How many twentieths more make a whole?

teaching_flow.title: Adding to a whole number
teacher_says: Look at this. One bar is 1 whole. We add 1 plus 1 and 3 fourths.
Start at 0. Travel 1 unit. Travel 1 more unit. You are at 2.
Now travel 3 fourths. Cut the space after 2 into 4 small units. Count 3.

teaching_flow.title: Add whole numbers first
teacher_says: Now 2 and 3 tenths plus 3.
Add the whole numbers first. Then show the fraction.
The fraction does not change. 2 plus 3 is 5. So the answer is 5 and 3 tenths.

teaching_flow.title: Subtract from 1
teacher_says: Start at 1. We subtract 1 fourth.
The answer is between 0 and 1. So the whole number part is 0.
Cut the line into fourths. Travel back 1 fourth. We land on 3 fourths.

teaching_flow.title: Subtract a fraction from 2
teacher_says: Start at 2. We subtract 3 fifths. We are not subtracting a whole number.
The answer is between 1 and 2. So the whole number part is 1.
Cut the space into fifths. Count back 3 fifths.

teaching_flow.title: Subtract a mixed number
teacher_says: Now 3 minus 1 and 2 thirds. First subtract the whole number 1. That leaves 2.
Then subtract 2 thirds from 2. The answer is between 1 and 2.

teaching_flow.title: Addition versus subtraction
teacher_says: Addition is quick. Add the whole numbers. Write the fraction.
Subtraction takes more thought. After subtracting the whole numbers, the answer is one smaller.
Find the fraction by counting up to the whole number.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Adding: whole numbers, then the fraction. Subtracting: the whole number part is one smaller, then count the fraction.

explanations.title: Add on the number line
explanations.text: Start at 0. Travel the whole numbers first. Then travel the fraction. Cut the space after the last whole number into equal small units. The fraction part stays the same.

explanations.title: Subtract on the number line
explanations.text: Start at the whole number. Ask: which two whole numbers will the answer lie between? That gives the whole number part. Cut the line into small units. Count back to find the fraction.

explanations.title: Count up to find the fraction
explanations.text: To find the fraction part, count up. For 1 minus some sevenths, count up in sevenths to reach 1. The sevenths you count are the fraction part.

explanations.title: When the fractions make a whole
explanations.text: Add the whole numbers first. Then add the fractions. If the fractions make 5 fifths, that is 1 more whole. Add it to the whole number.

objective.text: Add fractions by making like units with numbers. Multiply the top and bottom by the same number.

big_idea.text: Multiply the top and bottom by the same number. The name changes, but the value stays the same.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A bottom number that both fractions can use.
A number that both numbers go into.
vocabulary.example: 10 is a common multiple of 2 and 5.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The top number. How many parts are picked.
The bottom number. How many equal parts in the whole.

intro.hook: Drawing rectangles is slow. What if you could do the same thing with just numbers?
intro.why_it_matters: Numbers are faster. And they show you exactly what changes and what stays the same.
intro.link_to_before: You already know how to add fractions with unlike units by drawing.
intro.today_goal: Today you will add fractions by making like units with numbers.

teaching_flow.title: Why numbers instead of drawing?
teacher_says: Drawing rectangles works, but it is slow.
Today we do the same thing with numbers. It is faster, and you see what changes.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up
teacher_says: Add like units first. 3 sevenths plus 3 sevenths is 6 sevenths.

teaching_flow.title: What happens when we cut the pieces?
teacher_says: Think of the rectangle for 1 half. It has 2 parts. 1 is selected.
Cut each part into 5 smaller parts. Now there are 5 times as many parts in the whole. That is 10.
And 5 times as many selected parts. That is 5.
So the units got smaller, but the value stayed the same.

teaching_flow.title: Write it as an equation
teacher_says: 1 half times 5 over 5 is 5 tenths.
We multiply the top and the bottom by the same number. We are multiplying by 1 in a different name: 5 fifths.
Do the same for 1 fifth. Multiply by 2 over 2. It becomes 2 tenths.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Do not say the fraction 'changes'. The name changes, the value stays the same.

teaching_flow.title: Other like units
teacher_says: Tenths is one like unit. Others work too: twentieths, thirtieths, fiftieths.
1 half is 10 twentieths. 1 fifth is 4 twentieths. 14 twentieths equals 7 tenths.

teaching_flow.title: A sum bigger than 1
teacher_says: Now add 1 half and 2 thirds. 2 thirds is more than 1 half. So we expect more than 1.
Like unit: sixths. 1 half is 3 sixths. 2 thirds is 4 sixths.
3 sixths plus 4 sixths is 7 sixths. That is 1 and 1 sixth.

teaching_flow.title: Bigger common units
teacher_says: 6 and 9 can make fifty-fourths if we multiply. But eighteenths is a larger unit that also works.
Try 5 sixths plus 5 ninths in eighteenths.
Now try three addends: the like unit must work for all three.

teaching_flow.title: When one bottom number fits in the other
teacher_says: Look at 1 fourth plus 3 eighths. Eighths come from fourths.
Change only the 1 fourth: 2 eighths. Then add.

teaching_flow.title: Multiply always? Not always the best
teacher_says: Multiplying the bottom numbers always works. It is not always the smallest unit.
Skip-count by the bigger bottom number until you hit a multiple of the other one.
Different units give the same amount, so both answers are right.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Find a like unit. Multiply the top and the bottom by the same number. Add. Simplify.

explanations.title: Cutting parts and counting
explanations.text: Take 1 half of a rectangle. Cut each part into 5 smaller parts. The whole has 5 times as many parts. The selected part has 5 times as many parts too. 1 half becomes 5 tenths.

explanations.title: Multiply by a form of 1
explanations.text: Multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number is like multiplying by 1. 5 over 5 is 1. So the value does not change. The unit gets smaller. There are more of them.

explanations.title: Choosing a like unit
explanations.text: A like unit is a common multiple of both bottom numbers. For halves and fifths: 10, 20, 30, 50. Any of them works. To find one, skip-count by the bigger bottom number. Stop at a multiple of the other.

big_idea.text: Add the wholes. Add the fractions with like units. If the fractions make more than 1, take out a new whole.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A whole number and a fraction together.
A bottom number both fractions share.
A whole you take out of a fraction that is more than 1.

intro.hook: What is 20 and 41 fortieths? It looks odd. A new whole is hiding in it.
intro.why_it_matters: Real totals often pass 2 or 3. You need to add big mixed numbers without errors.
intro.link_to_before: You can already add fractions with unlike units, and sums up to 2.
intro.today_goal: Today you will add mixed numbers when the answer is more than 2.

teaching_flow.title: Big numbers, same idea
teacher_says: Today the numbers get big. Think of 20 and 41 fortieths. It looks scary.
But we use the same moves you already know. Add wholes. Make like units. Add fractions.
The trick is a new whole that hides inside the fraction.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up from the punch problem
teacher_says: Mrs. Lui mixes juice for a party. Some units are thirds. Some are fourths.
She adds like units first. 3 fourths plus 3 fourths is 6 fourths. That is 1 and 1 half.
Then she adds that to the 2 cups from thirds. 2 plus 1 and 1 half is 3 and 1 half cups.

teaching_flow.title: Guess first, then solve
teacher_says: Before we solve, we guess the size of the answer. Add the wholes. Then look at the fractions.
Take 2 and 4 fifths plus 1 and 1 half. Wholes: 3. 4 fifths is close to 1. Adding 1 half gives more than 1.
So the sum is more than 4. It is between 4 and 5.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: is the fraction part more than 1 or less than 1? That decides which whole number the sum passes.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 1: split wholes and fractions
teacher_says: We can add the wholes and the fractions separately. We can do this in any order.
Take 2 and 1 fifth plus 1 and 1 half. Wholes: 2 plus 1 is 3. Fractions: 1 fifth plus 1 half.
We cannot add fifths and halves. Make like units: tenths. 1 fifth is 2 tenths. 1 half is 5 tenths.
2 tenths plus 5 tenths is 7 tenths. Add the 3: 3 and 7 tenths.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 2: the fractions make a new whole
teacher_says: Now change 1 fifth to 4 fifths. Wholes: still 3.
4 fifths is 8 tenths. 1 half is 5 tenths. 8 tenths plus 5 tenths is 13 tenths.
13 tenths is more than 1 whole. 10 tenths is 1 whole. So it is 1 and 3 tenths.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 3: guess close to the whole
teacher_says: Try 5 and 5 sixths plus 2 and 2 fifths. The wholes make 7.
5 sixths is just 1 sixth short of 1 whole. 2 fifths is bigger than 1 sixth. So the fractions make more than 1.
The sum is a bit more than 8. It is between 8 and 9, close to 8.
Now solve. Like unit: thirtieths. 5 sixths is 25 thirtieths. 2 fifths is 12 thirtieths. Total: 37 thirtieths, which is 1 and 7 thirtieths.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 4: two big fractions
teacher_says: Try 4 and 3 fifths plus 5 and 3 fourths. The wholes make 9.
3 fifths is more than 1 half. 3 fourths is more than 1 half. Two things over 1 half add to more than 1.
So the sum is between 10 and 11.
Now solve with twentieths. 3 fifths is 12 twentieths. 3 fourths is 15 twentieths. Total 27 twentieths, which is 1 and 7 twentieths. The answer is 10 and 7 twentieths.

teaching_flow.title: Problems 5 and 6: more than one choice of unit
teacher_says: Sometimes there is more than one good like unit. Take 4 and 5 eighths plus 3 and 1 half.
Julia multiplies the bottom numbers and gets sixteenths. Curtis sees that eighths come from halves. Only 1 half needs to change.
Both get the same value. Try the eighths way.
Last, a time problem. Sixtieths can be turned into minutes. 1 hour is 60 minutes. So 28 sixtieths of an hour is 28 minutes.

teaching_flow.title: How do you know there is a new whole?
teacher_says: Look at the top and the bottom number of the fraction part. If the top is bigger, there is a new whole inside.
Take 20 and 41 fortieths. 40 fortieths is 1. So it is 21 and 1 fortieth.
Always guess before and check after. A guess catches big mistakes.

teaching_flow.title: Check the wrong guess
teacher_says: Clayton adds 2 and 3 fourths plus 3 and 2 thirds. He says the answer is between 5 and 6, because 2 plus 3 is 5.
Look at the fractions. 3 fourths and 2 thirds are each more than 1 half. Together they make more than 1.
So the sum is more than 6. Clayton forgot to look at the fractions.

explanations.title: Add wholes and fractions separately

explanations.title: Guess before solving
explanations.text: Add the wholes. Then check if the fractions together are more than 1 or less than 1. That tells you which two whole numbers the sum is between. Use 1 half as a helper. Two fractions each over 1 half add to more than 1.

explanations.title: Choose a like unit
explanations.text: Any common multiple works. Multiplying the bottom numbers always works. If one bottom number goes into the other, change only one fraction. For time, sixtieths are handy because 1 hour is 60 minutes.

objective.text: Subtract fractions by making like units with numbers.

big_idea.text: Rename both fractions with the same bottom number. Then subtract the tops. The value does not change when you rename.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A bottom number both fractions share.
Fractions with different names and the same value.
The answer when you subtract.

intro.hook: You subtract unlike fractions by drawing. What if you could skip the drawing?
intro.why_it_matters: An equation is faster than a picture. It also shows each step clearly.
intro.link_to_before: Last lesson you added fractions by making like units with numbers.
intro.today_goal: Today you will subtract fractions by making like units with numbers.

teaching_flow.title: From drawing to numbers
teacher_says: You can already subtract unlike fractions by drawing. Today we do it with numbers.
It uses the same idea as adding. Make like units. Then work with the tops.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up
teacher_says: 2 minus 1 half is 1 and 1 half. 7 minus 1 half is 6 and 1 half.
Like units are easy. 3 sevenths minus 1 seventh is 2 sevenths.
4 sevenths plus 3 sevenths is 7 sevenths. That is 1.

teaching_flow.title: Meredith at the movies (adding with numbers)
teacher_says: Meredith spent 2 fifths on a ticket. She spent 3 sevenths on popcorn. How much did she spend?
Fifths and sevenths do not match. Make like units. 5 times 7 is 35. So thirty-fifths.
2 fifths times 7 over 7 is 14 thirty-fifths. 3 sevenths times 5 over 5 is 15 thirty-fifths.
14 plus 15 is 29. She spent 29 thirty-fifths. That is less than 1, because the top is smaller than the bottom.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 1: subtract with like units
teacher_says: Now subtract. 1 third minus 1 fifth. We could draw two rectangles. Today we use an equation.
Like unit for thirds and fifths: fifteenths. 1 third is 5 fifteenths. 1 fifth is 3 fifteenths.
5 fifteenths minus 3 fifteenths is 2 fifteenths. Subtract the tops. Keep the bottom.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Do not say the fractions 'change'. They are renamed. The value stays the same.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 2: rename both fractions
teacher_says: Now 3 fifths minus 1 sixth. Multiply 3 fifths by 6 over 6. Multiply 1 sixth by 5 over 5.
Each fraction is the same value, in smaller units. 3 fifths is 18 thirtieths. 1 sixth is 5 thirtieths.
18 thirtieths minus 5 thirtieths is 13 thirtieths.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 3: three ways to solve one problem
teacher_says: Take 1 and 3 fourths minus 3 fifths. There are three good ways.
Way 1: take 3 fifths from 1. That leaves 2 fifths. Then add the 3 fourths. 2 fifths plus 3 fourths is 1 and 3 twentieths.
Way 2: subtract only the fractions. 3 fourths minus 3 fifths is 3 twentieths. Then add the whole number 1.
Way 3: write 1 as 4 fourths. 4 fourths plus 3 fourths is 7 fourths. Then 7 fourths minus 3 fifths.
All three give 1 and 3 twentieths. Pick the way that feels easy.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Go back to Way 2. It has the fewest steps. Subtract the fractions. Then add the whole.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The source names three methods but the numbers were lost. A matching problem was rebuilt so all three methods give the same answer.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 4: check with a number line
teacher_says: Take 3 and 3 fifths minus 2 and 1 half. First, guess. 3 minus 2 is 1. 3 fifths is a bit more than 1 half. So a bit more than 1.
Use tenths. 3 fifths is 6 tenths. 1 half is 5 tenths. 6 tenths minus 5 tenths is 1 tenth.
The answer is 1 and 1 tenth. Use a number line from 0 to 4. Jump back 2, then back 1 half. You land near 1.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 5: a big fraction minus a small one
teacher_says: Take 4 and 3 fourths minus 2 and 1 sixth. 3 fourths is much bigger than 1 sixth. The answer is between 2 and 3.
Use twenty-fourths. 3 fourths is 18 twenty-fourths. 1 sixth is 4 twenty-fourths. 18 minus 4 is 14.
14 twenty-fourths is the same as 7 twelfths. The units are twice as big, so you need half as many.
The answer is 2 and 7 twelfths.

teaching_flow.title: You do not have to multiply both fractions
teacher_says: George thinks you must always multiply the bottom numbers. That always works. But it is not always the smartest.
Look at 3 fourths minus 3 eighths. Eighths come from fourths. Change only the 3 fourths into 6 eighths.
A smaller like unit makes the numbers easier. Sometimes a bigger unit is useful too, like sixtieths for minutes.

teaching_flow.title: Always check the size
teacher_says: Some students are so fast that they add by mistake. Then the answer is bigger than the start.
A subtraction answer must be smaller than the number you started with. Check this every time.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Make like units. Subtract the tops. Keep the bottom. Simplify. Check that the answer is smaller than the start.

explanations.title: Same like-unit idea as adding
explanations.text: To subtract unlike fractions, rename both so the bottom numbers match. Multiply the top and bottom by the same number. Then subtract the tops and keep the bottom.

explanations.title: Renaming keeps the value
explanations.text: Multiplying the top and bottom by the same number is like multiplying by 1. The fraction is cut into smaller units. The value is the same.

explanations.title: Three ways to subtract from a mixed number
explanations.text: Way 1: take the fraction from 1, then add the rest. Way 2: subtract the fractions, then add the whole number. Way 3: write the whole as a fraction, then subtract. All give the same value.

explanations.title: Choose the like unit
explanations.text: Multiplying the bottom numbers always works. A smaller unit may be easier. If one bottom number goes into the other, change only one fraction. Larger units can be rewritten to smaller numbers later.

objective.text: Subtract fractions greater than or equal to 1.

big_idea.text: To subtract from a number bigger than 1, break a whole into smaller units. Or take the whole numbers first. Both give the same answer.

intro.hook: How did you subtract 14 minus 9 in Grade 1? You broke a ten into ones.
intro.why_it_matters: The same move works for fractions. Once you see it, subtraction stops being scary.
intro.link_to_before: Last lesson you subtracted fractions by making like units with numbers.
intro.today_goal: Today you will subtract fractions from numbers that are 1 or more.

teaching_flow.title: Subtracting with more than one unit
teacher_says: Think about 14 minus 9. You break a ten into ones. Then it is easy.
Today we do the same with fractions. We break 1 whole into smaller units.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up
teacher_says: 7 sevenths minus 3 sevenths is 4 sevenths. 1 minus 1 half is 1 half.
1 and 1 fifth is the same as 6 fifths.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 1: 1 and 1 fifth minus 1 half
teacher_says: We start with 1 and 1 fifth. We take away 1 half. 1 half is bigger than 1 fifth. So we need to break the whole.
Look at a number line. The answer is less than 1.
Method 1: take 1 half from 1. That leaves 1 half. Now add back the 1 fifth. 1 half plus 1 fifth is 7 tenths.
Method 2: 1 and 1 fifth is 6 fifths, or 12 tenths. 12 tenths minus 5 tenths is 7 tenths.
Both methods give 7 tenths.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: which is the whole? Which is the part you take away? Draw the line again.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The source tells the child to take the half from 1, and from 1 and 1 fifth. The exact numbers were lost and are rebuilt.

teaching_flow.title: The same fractions, switched
teacher_says: Now 1 and 1 half minus 1 fifth. This time we take a small fraction from a bigger one. No need to break the whole.
Use tenths. 1 half is 5 tenths. 1 fifth is 2 tenths. 5 tenths minus 2 tenths is 3 tenths. Add the 1.
The answer is 1 and 3 tenths. It is between 1 and 2.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 2: guess, then solve two ways
teacher_says: Take 3 and 1 fourth minus 1 and 3 fifths. Guess first on a number line. 3 minus 1 is 2. We take a little more, so the answer is between 1 and 2.
Method 1: take 1 and 3 fifths from 3. That is 1 and 2 fifths. Add back the 1 fourth. The answer is 1 and 13 twentieths.
Method 2: take the whole 1 first. That leaves 2 and 1 fourth. Then take 3 fifths. You get the same answer.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source says Problems 2 and 3 have the same pattern: number line, estimate, two methods. Numbers are generated.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 4: which is greater?
teacher_says: Take 4 and 1 half minus 3 and 2 thirds. First, which is greater: 1 half or 2 thirds?
Use like units: sixths. 1 half is 3 sixths. 2 thirds is 4 sixths. So 2 thirds is greater.
That means we cannot take 2 thirds from 1 half. We will use a number bond.
Method 1: take 3 and 2 thirds from 4. That is 1 third. Add back the 1 half. 1 third plus 1 half is 5 sixths.
Method 2: take away the whole 3 first. That leaves 1 and 1 half. Then take away 2 thirds. You get 5 sixths again.

teaching_flow.title: Subtraction in every grade
teacher_says: Look at 324 minus 198. Break 324 into 200 and 124. 200 minus 198 is 2. Add the 124. The answer is 126.
With units: 1 foot 3 inches minus 7 inches. Break 1 foot into 12 inches. 12 minus 7 is 5. Add the 3. You get 8 inches.
With fractions: break 1 whole into sevenths, take 3 sevenths, then add back.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Find the whole and the part taken away. Break a whole into small units if you need to. Subtract. Add back what is left. Check on a number line.

explanations.title: Take from 1, then add back
explanations.text: Sometimes the fraction you take away is too big for the fraction part. Then take it from 1 whole. Add back the leftover. Example: 1 and 1 fifth minus 1 half is 1 half plus 1 fifth.

explanations.title: Rename the whole
explanations.text: Write the mixed number as one fraction. 1 and 1 fifth is 6 fifths, or 12 tenths. Then subtract with like units.

explanations.title: Subtract whole numbers first
explanations.text: You can take the whole number away first. Then take the fraction away from what is left. Sometimes this is faster.

explanations.title: The same idea in every grade
explanations.text: Grade 1: 14 minus 9 breaks a ten. Grade 2: 324 minus 198 splits 324. Grade 3: 1 foot becomes 12 inches. Grade 4: 1 kg becomes 1,000 g. Grade 5: 1 whole becomes sevenths.

objective.text: Use fraction benchmark numbers to assess reasonableness of addition and subtraction equations.

big_idea.text: Compare each fraction to 0, 1 half and 1. It shows if a sum is more or less than a benchmark. You see this before you solve.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A friendly number you compare to.
A close guess made by thinking.
vocabulary.example: 1 half plus 3 fourths is more than 1.

vocabulary.kid_definition: An answer that makes sense.
vocabulary.example: A subtraction answer smaller than the start.

intro.hook: Is 1 half plus 3 fourths more than 1? Can you tell without any paper?
intro.why_it_matters: A quick guess helps you catch mistakes. It also saves time.
intro.link_to_before: For two weeks you learned ways to add and subtract unlike fractions.
intro.today_goal: Today you will use benchmark numbers to check if answers make sense.

teaching_flow.title: Can you know without solving?
teacher_says: Some answers you can guess in your head. Is 1 half plus 3 fourths more than 1? Yes! You do not need paper.
Today we learn to estimate with benchmarks. Benchmarks are friendly numbers: 0, 1 half and 1.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up with decimals
teacher_says: 1 half is 5 tenths. As a decimal, it is 0.5. 3 and 1 half is 3.5.
Think of money. 1 half is 50 cents. 3 fourths is 75 cents.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 1: more than 1?
teacher_says: Look at 1 half plus 3 fourths. 3 fourths is more than 1 half. So the sum is more than 1.
Like money: 50 cents plus 75 cents is more than 1 dollar.
Now check. 1 half is 2 fourths. 2 fourths plus 3 fourths is 5 fourths. That is 1 and 1 fourth.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Say the benchmark question aloud each time: is it closer to 0, 1 half, or 1?

teaching_flow.title: Problem 2: subtraction
teacher_says: Look at 1 and 1 fifth minus 3 fourths. 3 fourths is bigger than 1 fifth. So we must take it from the 1 whole.
We start just over 1. We take away almost 1. So the answer is less than 1.
Check with twentieths. 1 and 1 fifth is 24 twentieths. 3 fourths is 15 twentieths. 24 minus 15 is 9. The answer is 9 twentieths.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 3: two small fractions
teacher_says: Look at 4 tenths plus 3 eighths. Half of 10 is 5. So 4 tenths is less than 1 half. Half of 8 is 4. So 3 eighths is less than 1 half.
Two things under 1 half add to less than 1. So the sum is less than 1.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is half of the bottom number? Is the top number smaller than that?

teaching_flow.title: Problem 4: close to 1 half
teacher_says: Look at 2 ninths plus 3 tenths. Both are less than 1 half. The sum is less than 1.
But is it more or less than 1 half? It is close. We have to check. 2 ninths is 20 ninetieths. 3 tenths is 27 ninetieths. The sum is 47 ninetieths.
1 half is 45 ninetieths. So the sum is a little more than 1 half.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Some estimates are close. When close, calculate. This teaches the limit of benchmark reasoning.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 6: subtraction and 1 half
teacher_says: Look at 4 fifths minus 1 sixth. Is it more than 1 half? 1 half plus 1 sixth is 2 thirds. 4 fifths is more than 2 thirds.
So 4 fifths minus 1 sixth is more than 1 half. Check: 24 thirtieths minus 5 thirtieths is 19 thirtieths. That is more than 15 thirtieths.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 7: which sum is greater?
teacher_says: Compare two sums. Left: 3 and 1 fifth plus 2 and 1 sixth. Right: 3 and 3 fourths plus 2 and 5 sixths.
First add the wholes. 3 plus 2 is 5 on each side. They are equal. So we look at the fractions.
On the left, 1 fifth and 1 sixth are close to 0. Together they are less than 1. On the right, 3 fourths and 5 sixths are close to 1. Together they are more than 1.
So the right side is greater.

teaching_flow.title: Why estimate?
teacher_says: Estimating before tells you what size to expect. Estimating after checks your work.
A baker needs 2 pounds of butter. She has 3 fourths, 3 fourths and 1 fourth. 3 fourths plus 3 fourths is 1 and 1 half. Add 1 fourth. That is 1 and 3 fourths. Not enough.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Ask: is each fraction closer to 0, 1 half or 1? Add or subtract the wholes first. Estimate. Then solve and check.

explanations.title: Benchmark numbers
explanations.text: A benchmark is a friendly number to compare with. For fractions, the benchmarks are 0, 1 half and 1. To decide, halve the bottom number. Compare the top number to it.

explanations.title: Two fractions and 1 half
explanations.text: Two fractions that are each more than 1 half add to more than 1. Two fractions that are each less than 1 half add to less than 1.

explanations.title: Compare the wholes, then the fractions
explanations.text: To compare two sums, add the wholes first. If the wholes are equal, estimate the fractions. Is each pair more than 1 or less than 1?

explanations.title: When the estimate is close
explanations.text: Sometimes a sum is close to a benchmark. Then you cannot decide by estimating. Make like units and check.

big_idea.text: First ask if the whole is given or missing. Group like units and look for pairs that make wholes. Then add or subtract.

vocabulary.kid_definition: One number in an addition or subtraction problem.
vocabulary.example: In 3 plus 2 plus 1, there are 3 terms.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The whole is the total. A part is a piece of it.
vocabulary.example: In 5 minus 2 equals 3, 5 is the whole.

intro.hook: What is 1 third plus 1 and 3 fifths plus 2 thirds plus 2 fifths? Looks long. But two pairs make wholes!
intro.why_it_matters: Long problems are easy if you look for friendly pairs and ask what is missing.
intro.link_to_before: You can add and subtract two fractions. Now there are many.
intro.today_goal: Today you will plan how to solve problems with many fractions.

teaching_flow.title: Many numbers, one story
teacher_says: Some problems have many numbers. They can look hard. Look for friends that make a whole.
Think of 1 third and 2 thirds. They make 1. That makes the problem easy.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up
teacher_says: 1 third plus 2 thirds is 1 whole. 2 and 1 half plus 1 and 1 half is 4.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 1: group the like units
teacher_says: Look at 1 third plus 1 and 3 fifths plus 2 thirds plus 2 fifths. We can add in any order.
Spot the thirds. 1 third and 2 thirds make 1 whole. Spot the fifths. 1 and 3 fifths and 2 fifths make 2 wholes.
Then 1 plus 2 is 3. No new like units needed.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: which fractions have the same bottom number? Put them together.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source numbers are lost. The idea is: group thirds into 1 whole and fifths into 2 wholes. 1 plus 2 is 3.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 2: whole minus many parts
teacher_says: Look at 5 and 7 eighths minus 7 eighths minus 1 and 1 half minus 1 half. The first number is the whole. The others are parts we take away.
Combine the parts first. 1 and 1 half plus 1 half is 2.
Take 7 eighths from 5 and 7 eighths. That is 5. Then take the 2. 5 minus 2 is 3.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 4: a missing part
teacher_says: Look at this. 1 and 3 fourths, plus a missing part, plus 2 and 1 fourth. The total is 6 and 1 half. A part is missing.
Add the parts you know. 1 and 3 fourths plus 2 and 1 fourth is 4. Then take 4 from 6 and 1 half. The missing part is 2 and 1 half.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: is the whole given? Then take all known parts away.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 5: a missing whole
teacher_says: Now a number minus 1 and 1 half minus 3 and 1 half equals 2 and 1 fourth. Here the whole is missing.
When the whole is missing, add all the parts. 1 and 1 half plus 3 and 1 half is 5. Add 2 and 1 fourth. The whole is 7 and 1 fourth.

teaching_flow.title: A word problem
teacher_says: DeAngelo needs 100 pounds of soil. He finds 3 cases. We know the whole. We want a missing part.
Add the 3 cases first. Then take the total from 100.

teaching_flow.title: What helped?
teacher_says: Group fractions to make whole numbers. Look for numbers in different forms.
Ask each time: is the whole given or missing? That decides add or subtract.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Is the whole given or missing? Group like units. Look for pairs that make wholes. Combine parts, then add or subtract.

explanations.title: Group like units to make wholes
explanations.text: Addition can be done in any order. Group fractions with the same bottom number. Look for pairs that make a whole, like 1 third and 2 thirds. Then add the wholes.

explanations.title: Whole and parts
explanations.text: Every problem has a whole and parts. If the whole is given, take the parts away. If the whole is missing, add the parts. This tells you whether to add or subtract.

explanations.title: Combine the parts first
explanations.text: When you take away many parts, add the parts together first. Then take one big part from the whole. It is fewer steps.

examples.text: Missing part: add the known parts, then subtract from the whole. Missing whole: add all the parts.

intro.hook: A race has three runners. You know the last runner's time. Can you find the winner's time?
intro.why_it_matters: Real problems tell a story. A drawing and a plan make them simple.

teaching_flow.title: Stories need a plan
teacher_says: Word problems with fractions are stories. Draw the story, then solve it in steps.
Today the problems have more than one step. And the answer may need minutes and seconds.

teaching_flow.title: Minutes and seconds
teacher_says: 1 minute is 60 seconds. A fraction of a minute turns into seconds if you multiply by 60.
7 twelfths of a minute is 35 seconds.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 1: the race
teacher_says: In a race, the second finisher crossed 1 and 1 fourth minutes after the winner. The third finisher was 1 and 1 third minutes behind the second. The third finisher took 34 and 1 sixth minutes. How long did the winner take?
Draw 3 bars. The winner is short. The second is longer by 1 and 1 fourth. The third is longer again by 1 and 1 third. Label the third bar 34 and 1 sixth.
We know the third time. So find the second time first. Subtract 1 and 1 third. That is 32 and 5 sixths.
Then find the winner. Subtract 1 and 1 fourth. That is 31 and 7 twelfths.
The question may ask for minutes and seconds. 7 twelfths of a minute is 35 seconds. The winner took 31 minutes 35 seconds.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 2: salt for the ice
teacher_says: John buys 10 kg of salt. He uses 3 and 1 fourth kg on the sidewalk. Then he uses 2 and 1 half kg on the driveway. How much is left?
Draw one whole tape. Label it 10. Cut it into 3 parts. One for the sidewalk. One for the driveway. A question mark for what is left.
Add the two used amounts. 3 and 1 fourth plus 2 and 1 half is 5 and 3 fourths. Take that from 10. 4 and 1 fourth is left.
Check by rounding. About 3 and about 2 and a half. 10 minus 5 and a half is about 4 and a half. Close to 4 and 1 fourth. It is reasonable.

teaching_flow.title: Gavin's quiz
teacher_says: Gavin has 20 minutes for a 3-problem quiz. He spends 9 and 3 fourths minutes on Problem 1. He spends 3 and 4 fifths minutes on Problem 2. How much is left for Problem 3?

Add the two known times in twentieths. Take the total from 20. Then change the fraction to seconds.

teaching_flow.title: Two ways to solve it
teacher_says: Student A used the 20 minutes to subtract the two times. Then changed the answer to minutes and seconds. Short.

big_idea.text: Use unit boxes. A fraction of the whole tells you how many equal units the whole has. Count units, then find 1 unit.

vocabulary.kid_definition: One small equal box you pick to count with.
The complete amount.
A piece of the whole.

intro.hook: Here is a piece of ribbon. It is 1 fourth of a whole ribbon. How long is the whole?
intro.why_it_matters: Knowing how a part fits in a whole helps with multiplying and dividing fractions soon.
intro.link_to_before: You have been adding and subtracting fractions of a whole.
intro.today_goal: Today you will work out the whole from a part, and compare lengths with units.

teaching_flow.title: Fractions of something
teacher_says: Usually we cut a shape to make a fraction. Today it is the other way round.
We are given a piece. It is a fraction of the whole. Our job is to find the whole.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up
teacher_says: A like unit for 3 and 2 is 6. Both 3 and 2 go into 6.
7 fourths breaks into 4 fourths and 3 fourths. That is 1 and 3 fourths.

teaching_flow.title: Question 1: a piece of ribbon
teacher_says: A ribbon piece is 1 fourth of the whole ribbon. 4 of these pieces make the whole. Draw 4 equal boxes.
Now the piece is 3 fourths of the whole. The piece has 3 equal units. The whole needs 1 more. The whole has 4 units.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source numbers lost. The idea: a piece that is a fraction of the whole. Draw the whole from the piece.

teaching_flow.title: Question 1c and 1d: comparing ribbons
teacher_says: Two ribbons. 1 third of A is equal to all of B. Let B be 1 unit. Then A is 3 units.
Three ribbons. C is half of D. E is twice D. Let C be 1 unit. Then D is 2 units. E is 4 units.

teaching_flow.title: Question 2: Robert's and Maria's wires
teacher_says: Half of Robert's wire equals 3 fourths of Maria's wire. Together they have 10 feet. How much longer is Robert's?
Let half of Robert's be 3 units. Then Robert's is 6 units. 3 fourths of Maria's is 3 units. So Maria's is 4 units.
6 plus 4 is 10 units. 10 units are 10 feet. So 1 unit is 1 foot. Robert's wire is 2 feet longer.

teaching_flow.title: Question 3: Sarah, Daniel and Chris
teacher_says: Half of Sarah's wire is equal to 2 fifths of Daniel's. Chris has 3 times as much as Sarah. In all they have 6 feet.
Let half of Sarah's be 2 units. Then Sarah's is 4 units. 2 units are 2 fifths of Daniel's. So Daniel's is 5 units.
Chris has 3 times Sarah's 4. That is 12 units. All together: 4, 5 and 12 are 21 units.
21 units are 6 feet. 1 unit is 6 over 21, or 2 sevenths of a foot. Sarah's has 4 units. That is 8 sevenths, or 1 and 1 seventh feet.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: if half of Sarah's is a box, how many boxes is Sarah's? Draw it.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The Debrief mentions '21 units in Problem 3'. These numbers are rebuilt to fit that.

teaching_flow.title: Roads
teacher_says: Three roads. B is 3 times as long as A. C is twice as long as B. Let A be 1 unit. Then B is 3 units. C is 6 units.
All together: 1, 3 and 6 are 10 units. A is 1 tenth of the total length.
B is 7 miles longer than A. B minus A is 2 units. So 2 units are 7 miles. 1 unit is 3 and 1 half miles. C is 6 units, which is 21 miles.

teaching_flow.title: What surprised you?
teacher_says: Think about how you usually make a fraction. Now think about today.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Make a unit box. Draw each bar with its units. Find the total units. Divide the total length by the total units. Then answer the question.

explanations.title: A piece that is a fraction of the whole
explanations.text: A piece may be 1 fourth of the whole. Then the whole is 4 of those pieces. A piece may be 3 fourths of the whole. Then the piece has 3 units and the whole has 4. A fraction tells you how many equal parts the whole has.

explanations.title: Use units
explanations.text: Pick one small box as 1 unit. Draw each bar with its units. Add all units. Divide the total length by the total units to get 1 unit. Multiply to find any bar.

explanations.title: Half of and times as long
explanations.text: Half of D equals C means D is 2 times C. Twice as long means 2 times the units. 3 times as long means 3 times the units.

explanations.title: A fraction is a division
explanations.text: A fraction is also a division. 6 divided by 21 is 6 over 21, which is 2 sevenths. The lesson links fractions to division, which comes next in the module.

A fraction of the whole tells you how many equal parts the whole has.
